feed.subtitle: Research papers and global crypto regulation, at a glance
feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: Weaver: a method that speeds up blockchain transactions by running them in parallel without waiting for state data.
entry.summary: Weaver: Unlocking Blockchain Transaction Parallelism through State-Decoupled Symbolic Execution arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents Weaver, a transaction processing approach that lets execution continue before concrete state values are fetched. It represents states as symbolic references, predicts branch directions through hierarchical symbolic pattern matching, and schedules individual expressions as soon as their dependencies are resolved. Evaluated on real Ethereum blocks and synthetic workloads from four dApps, it achieves 41% to 63% higher throughput than state-of-the-art parallel engines and up to 7.5 times that of serial execution.

entry.title: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid-Feasible, Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
entry.summary: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading arXiv · Nov 4, 2026GRIDSHIELD is a blockchain-based peer-to-peer energy trading system that keeps bids sealed while proving that cleared trades respect grid constraints. It clears trades with an order-independent batch program, so a compromised operator cannot profit by reordering them, and uses an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof to verify feasibility without trusted setup. The paper also introduces a fairness metric that assigns curtailment according to each party's responsibility for congestion, and evaluates the system on a Hyperledger Fabric network across four feeders.

entry.title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant reputation system for autonomous agent marketplaces
entry.summary: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper examines whether existing onchain payment histories can produce provider ratings that resist Sybil attacks, where one actor creates many fake identities. The authors model 66 million agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains over 157 days as a bipartite graph linking buyers and providers. They propose three Sybil-resistant rating algorithms, including a max-flow rating and two relaxed variants. Against simulated adversaries, manipulating ratings costs 20% of the affected buyers' total spend and is about 23 times harder than the standard collaborative filtering similarity rule.

entry.title: MuCPay: A Scriptless Multi-Party Protocol for Oracle-Based Conditional Payments
entry.summary: MuCPay: Breaking the Quadratic Bottleneck in Scriptless Multi-Party Oracle-Based Conditional Payments IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents MuCPay, a multi-party protocol for conditional payments triggered by real-world events via oracles, aimed at decentralized finance. It uses hash-bound adaptor multi-signatures (HB-AMS) to combine parties' conditional authorizations into one compact joint pre-signature, with scriptless settlement on Bitcoin compatible with BIP340. The authors prove concurrent new-message unforgeability and early-settlement resistance under static corruption with one honest signer, in an algebraic random-oracle model. For 128 parties and 16 outcomes, settlement uses a single 64-byte signature.

entry.title: Archive certificates that compress ML-DSA-87 blockchain signatures
entry.summary: Archive Certificates for ML-DSA-87 Authorizations from an Exact Bounded Relation IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026The paper proposes an archive certificate that shrinks long-term storage of ML-DSA-87 transaction signatures on a blockchain. It is a single hash-based proof that the prover knows canonical FIPS 204 signatures on the recorded messages for a range of validated blocks. For 65,536 signatures, the measured size is about 104 to 127 bytes per signature, versus 4,627 bytes raw, at the cost of a slow prover and a verifier slower than native verification. The authors give extraction error bounds in classical and quantum random oracle models and note that an external review is outstanding.

entry.title: Shielded Bitcoin: a protocol for private transfers directly on Bitcoin's base layer
entry.summary: Shielded Bitcoin: Private Transfers on the Bitcoin L1 IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents Shielded Bitcoin, a protocol for private Bitcoin transfers on the base layer that requires no changes to Bitcoin consensus. Value is held as encrypted notes, spends are marked with public nullifiers, and validity is proven with zero-knowledge proofs. All protocol data is published on Bitcoin, and shielded state is rebuilt off-chain by replaying accepted transfers in Bitcoin order.

entry.title: Blockchain-anchored proactive share refresh for dynamic threshold services
entry.summary: Blockchain-Anchored Proactive Refresh for Dynamic Threshold Services IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper addresses long-lived threshold services that must admit new participants, refresh shares against mobile adversaries, and let offline participants recover missed updates. It shows that tracking exposure only for committed epochs is insufficient, and it instead budgets security per fine-grained state, including aborted refresh attempts, using an append-only release ledger. Encrypted update records are stored in blockchain blob storage, and an on-chain bisection dispute protocol identifies faulty records. An end-to-end Rust implementation on an EVM chain benchmarks lifecycles with up to 1,280 participants, reporting sub-second group recovery and practical gas costs.

entry.title: Verifying data on Bitcoin with FlatMerkle commitments and refutable proofs
entry.summary: Verifiable Data on Bitcoin: FlatMerkle Commitments, Refutable Proofs, and FlatChecks IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026The paper presents a method for publishing data on Bitcoin and verifying its properties on-chain, even if the publisher may lie. The data is stored in a FlatMerkle format within a transaction annex or output, and disputes reduce to a few SHA-256 compressions and one Schnorr signature check. Two examples are given: a toy layer-2 batch of signed transfers and a Bitcoin header-chain light client, with their dispute costs in vbytes.

entry.title: Private accounts with less validator work via a hybrid state model
entry.summary: Private Accounts Without O(N) Work Through a Hybrid State Model IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026The paper argues that in account-balance-vector designs, hiding which accounts changed forces every private transfer to update global state indistinguishably, so validator work grows linearly with the number of accounts. It proposes separating state representation from execution model, and presents Miden, an Ethereum Layer 2 that uses persistent accounts for programmability, asynchronous notes for value transfer, and client-side proving for execution. Validators verify proofs and update commitments without re-executing transactions, keeping per-transaction work logarithmic in the number of accounts.

entry.title: Proving the Wrong Program: Compiler Bugs as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
entry.summary: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees arXiv · Nov 3, 2026A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, usually Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. This paper presents the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to the SP1 and Jolt zkVMs, assembling 88 known rustc and LLVM bugs with Rust reproducers. Of these, 48 cause SP1 guests and 46 cause Jolt guests to commit wrong outputs. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident, but an attacker can deliberately trigger these bugs by contributing crafted code. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first empirical study of miscompilations threatening zkVM guarantees, reproducing 88 known bugs on SP1 and Jolt and showing LLM-crafted triggering patches.

entry.title: How market volatility reacts to past price trends, measured by time lag in crypto and stocks
entry.summary: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper measures, at minute resolution, how market volatility responds to a preceding price trend as a function of lag, and examines the asymmetry of that response. The sample covers trades in three large cryptocurrencies on one exchange and three large US stocks plus an S&P 500 ETF from 2020 to 2026. The asymmetry is split under time reversal into T-even and T-odd parts, and the authors report a detectable T-odd part for the cryptocurrencies but none for the equities at a 20-minute lag.

entry.title: Rechecking Elliptic++, a Bitcoin Fraud Dataset, Without Future Data Leaks
entry.summary: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Elliptic++ is a widely used benchmark dataset for Bitcoin forensic analysis, but its split does not respect time order, letting future information leak into training. The authors recover the exact definitions of its 55 address-level features by linking to public ledger data, then recompute them using a time-based split by each address's first appearance. With leakage removed, the random forest's F1 score on the illicit class drops from 0.846 to 0.291, and it no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify temporal leakage in Elliptic++, reconstruct feature definitions via public ledger linkage, and report the illicit-class F1 for random forest dropping from 0.846 to 0.291.

entry.title: Attacks That Stop Messages Reaching Nodes in P2P Gossip Networks
entry.summary: Attacking P2P Networks: Liveness Attacks on the GossipSub and DOG Gossip Protocols arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how two peer-to-peer gossip protocols, GossipSub (used by Ethereum) and DOG (designed for CometBFT), hold up against attackers who only aim to keep honest nodes from receiving fresh messages. For GossipSub, the authors show that a few geographically distributed nodes with a latency advantage can capture the peer-scoring metric for first message deliveries and separate a constant fraction of nodes from the honest mesh. For DOG, they show a single physical node can disable all forwarding routes, leaving only direct publisher-to-neighbor delivery, and they verify this attack in a simulated network. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report liveness attacks exploiting GossipSub's First Message Deliveries scoring and DOG's route filtering, verified in simulation, with cost and mitigation analysis.

entry.title: Preregistered comparison of zero-shot forecasting models for Nordic carbon intensity
entry.summary: Zero-shot time-series foundation models against the Khepri v1.5 baselines for 96-hour carbon-intensity forecasts in nine Nordic bidding zones: a preregistered comparison arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This preregistered study compares three zero-shot time-series foundation models with the Khepri v1.5 SARIMA and GBM baselines for 96-hour forecasts of hourly carbon intensity across nine Nordic bidding zones. On the 2025 test, all three models have lower zone-averaged MAPE than both baselines and beat SARIMA in all nine zones. On a 14-origin holdout from October 2026 the differences point the same way but lie within the preregistered minimum detectable effect, so they are reported as not determined.

entry.title: RegionFence: adaptive concurrency control that speeds up parallel transaction processing on blockchains.
entry.summary: RegionFence: Adaptive Concurrency Control for Blockchain Parallel Transaction Execution arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Smart contract execution limits blockchain throughput, and most parallel engines use one concurrency policy per block, forcing whole transactions to re-execute or wait. This paper proposes RegionFence, which splits transactions into regions, uses run-time fences to decide how each region handles conflicts, and applies intra-block and inter-block online learning to anticipate conflicts while preserving serial-equivalent results. Implemented in go-ethereum and evaluated on Ethereum mainnet blocks from five years, it reports a 9.2x overall speedup over single-core execution on 64 cores. It outperforms OCC by 2.9–5.4x and PCC by 3.9–9.4x across the tested periods.

entry.title: A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference
entry.summary: A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper proposes the Open Inference Market (OIM), a peer-to-peer system in which individuals and small institutions contribute idle GPUs to AI inference. Its core mechanism, earnings as collateral, has workers deliver results without knowing whether they will be audited, with unsettled earnings held as collateral during a challenge window and forfeited entirely if cheating is confirmed. In a simplified model with example parameters, about 0.3 replays per worker per day make cheating unprofitable for a rational worker.

entry.title: AIDA: An AI Outage Registry Tracking Failures and On-Chain MEV Activity
entry.summary: AIDA: An AI Outage Registry with Evidence from On-Chain MEV arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper introduces the AI Incident and Disruption Archive (AIDA), a registry of 5,868 deduplicated outage incidents across 30 AI providers from 2025 to 2026, with foundation-model incidents verified against primary sources. The authors pair it with verified maximal extractable value (MEV) transaction data on Ethereum and Base. They find that active arbitrage addresses quadrupled from late 2024 to late 2026 while sandwich attackers declined, and execution stayed concentrated among the top fifty addresses. During AI outages, the release of new trading code slowed, while already-deployed bots continued trading.

entry.title: Attack Patterns in Cross-chain Bridges: A Trust-based Empirical Analysis
entry.summary: Attack Patterns in Cross-chain Bridges: A Trust-based Empirical Analysis arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper empirically studies 48 real-world cross-chain bridge attacks from January 2022 to August 2026. It proposes six attack patterns, each defined by the trust assumption the attacker violates, and maps them to five functional domains of bridges. On the primary loss basis, Proof Forgery and Credential Seizure account for 86.2% of losses, and the Verification and Governance and Operations domains hold 93.9%.

entry.title: Authorization design to limit crypto withdrawal losses if a backend is compromised
entry.summary: Intent-Bound Authorization for Cryptocurrency Withdrawals Under Backend Compromise arXiv · Oct 31, 2026The paper proposes the Intent-Bound Withdrawal Authorization Protocol (IWAP), in which an independent enforcement layer checks customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload evidence, and a single-use spending reservation before signing. The authors give conditional arguments for intent preservation, replay resistance, and a fixed-epoch exposure bound. A Python reference monitor tested on synthetic records shows that an independent budget still limits admitted exposure even when the intent authority is compromised. The study evaluates a normalized policy model, not any deployed custody platform.

entry.title: Beyond price: analyzing economic-state manipulation flaws in DeFi
entry.summary: Price is Only the Symptom: Understanding and Analyzing Economic-State Manipulation Vulnerabilities in DeFi arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper empirically studies economic-state manipulation (ESM) vulnerabilities in decentralized finance, using 276 real-world attacks and 91 Code4rena audit findings. It proposes a cause-oriented taxonomy with four primary categories and eleven subcategories. The authors find these vulnerabilities often involve violations of protocol accounting, AMM state consistency, and execution-time constraints, not just price manipulation. Among seven evaluated detection approaches, the best identified only 50.4% of real-world attacks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a cause-oriented taxonomy of economic-state manipulation, evaluated on 276 real attacks and 91 audit findings across seven detection approaches.

entry.title: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum
entry.summary: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum arXiv · Oct 30, 2026This paper examines a new attack enabled by EIP-7702, which lets externally owned accounts temporarily delegate execution to arbitrary contract code. In the described attack, a victim is delegated to a malicious sweeper contract that redirects incoming ETH to an attacker-controlled address. The authors present the first formal analysis of this attack model and introduce SweeperHunter, a transaction-analysis framework for detecting it. Analyzing ten months of Ethereum mainnet data, they identify millions of malicious delegations, tens of thousands of attack transactions, and 508 sweeper contracts, and propose mitigation strategies. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give the first formal analysis of EIP-7702 ether redirection attacks and report a detection framework that found over 20,000 attack transactions on Ethereum mainnet.

entry.title: Classifying Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using On-Chain Behavior and Proof-of-Reserves
entry.summary: On-Chain Behavioral Signatures for Classifying Centralized Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using Proof-of-Reserves arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper builds a classifier for identifying Ethereum addresses belonging to centralized exchanges, using Proof-of-Reserves disclosures to label roughly 3.03 million addresses from 15 exchanges and five non-exchange categories. It derives 58 on-chain behavioral features and tests LightGBM against logistic regression under a leave-one-exchange-out protocol. LightGBM outperformed logistic regression across all five lookback windows, and SHAP analysis highlights gas behavior, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as key signals.

entry.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Auditable Open Federated Learning
entry.summary: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning arXiv · Oct 30, 2026This paper presents AuditFL, a clearing layer for federated learning in open settings that uses smart contracts to make the coordinator's decisions auditable. Training and aggregation run off chain, with model artifacts stored in an off-chain store and only content identifiers and economic state recorded on chain. On full MNIST with non-IID splits, 12 rounds and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the learning trajectory of plain federated learning. Stress tests with dropouts, invalid updates and unavailable artifacts reduce participation but still finalize rounds with small accuracy changes.

entry.title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
entry.summary: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems arXiv · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies locking and unlocking in certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay when balances are shared among several debiting accounts. The authors prove that no unlock rule is safe unless certificate formation is visible to validators. They propose a hybrid protocol that keeps the client-driven path for personal accounts, while shared resources are certified by a two-phase ECHO and READY broadcast. When concurrent debits conflict, validators freeze the affected resource version and resolve it with one agreement instance. The protocol is proven to satisfy consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness, and composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.

entry.title: A coordination layer aligning incentives and trust for blockchain interoperability
entry.summary: An Incentive-Aligned Trust-Centric Coordination Layer for Heterogeneous Blockchain Interoperability arXiv · Oct 30, 2026This paper proposes a coordination architecture that handles cross-domain trust and privacy separately from underlying blockchain protocols, without requiring protocol changes. It combines cryptographic unlinkability with incentive-compatible relay selection, using stake-weighted participation and accumulated reputation. The authors formalize an adversarial model and analyze robustness against Sybil attacks, collusion, and stake concentration. Simulations examine trade-offs among quorum thresholds, reputation memory, and anonymity parameters.

entry.title: Overview of blockchains where several proposers add transactions at once
entry.summary: SoK: Multiple Concurrent Proposer Blockchains IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026This survey paper reviews multiple concurrent proposer (MCP) protocols, in which several parties contribute transactions to the same ledger update. It describes a common architecture covering transaction receipt through state finality, and identifies four direct MCP families. The paper compares these with constrained assembly, where several parties restrict a block built by one party, across 39 configurations. It concludes that additional proposers alone do not guarantee transaction inclusion.

entry.title: Sybil-Proof Generalized Adaptive Clinching for Blockchain Market Design
entry.summary: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026This paper introduces a generalized adaptive clinching framework and proves it is Sybil-robust incentive compatible: a bidder gains nothing by splitting its budget across any finite number of identities, provided the aggregate reported budget does not exceed its enforceable true budget. Motivated by blockchain decentralized finance, the authors design a new two-asset automated market maker mechanism that supports two-sided markets and state-dependent supply functions. They show it satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility and a relaxed Pareto optimality, and argue these guarantees are essentially the best possible given known and new impossibility results. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove Sybil-robust incentive compatibility for generalized adaptive clinching and design a two-sided AMM mechanism, with theoretical results compared against impossibility bounds.

entry.title: Sparse autoencoders as a diversification tool for crypto returns
entry.summary: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns arXiv · Oct 29, 2026This paper uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to describe daily returns of many cryptocurrencies with only a few active features. In a time-ordered evaluation against common benchmarks, SAE portfolios show consistently lower volatility, linked to lower correlations among selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted returns, and its factor identities are unstable across training runs.

entry.title: DICE: A decentralized, incentive-driven federated learning method for efficiently customizing pretrained models in Web3.
entry.summary: DICE: Decentralized Incentive-driven Federated Learning for Efficient & Scalable Customization of Pretrained Models in Web3 arXiv · Oct 29, 2026The paper presents DICE, a blockchain-based federated learning algorithm for customizing large pretrained models among Web3 participants. It uses dynamic progressive learning and model slice verification so that participants unable to deploy the full model can still take part. It also introduces a tree-structured committee consensus protocol and an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to support more data holders. The authors report that theoretical analysis and experiments on vision and language models demonstrate its efficiency, effectiveness, and security.

entry.title: Measuring Where Intent Is Lost When AI Agents Write Smart Contracts
entry.summary: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper examines whether AI agents that write smart contracts from plain-English descriptions actually produce code that behaves as requested. The authors compare an AI-written contract with the original on the same transactions and find that common AI judges and standard analysis tools miss obvious mistakes. They propose asking the client clarifying questions before code generation and checking the result against an independently written executable answer key, which they report works far better than reviewing or patching afterwards. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose asking clarifying questions before generation and checking against an independent executable answer key, reporting results on 600 tasks across three models and releasing tools.

entry.title: MEV: A multi-event video dataset for generating long, continuous video takes
entry.summary: MEV: A Multi-Event Video Dataset for Long-Take Generation arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper introduces MEV, a dataset of real-world videos in which subjects perform a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping events, with precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations. The authors also present an annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events and produces structured captions at both global and event levels. Under an event-centric evaluation protocol, fine-tuning on MEV with temporally grounded event conditioning is reported to improve event transitions and content coherence in long-take generation.
